facts.map-skills: Lesson facts to rely on: a map is a drawing of a place from above; a compass rose shows directions; cardinal directions are north, south, east, west; intermediate directions lie halfway between them (north-east, north-west, south-east, south-west); opposite directions (if A is east of B, B is west of A); most maps have north at the top unless the compass rose shows otherwise; a globe is a round model of Earth showing continents and oceans more accurately; maps are flat, easy to carry and can show more local detail.
facts.latitude-longitude: Lesson facts to rely on: latitude and longitude are imaginary lines forming a grid on maps and globes, used to locate places and measured in degrees (°); lines of latitude run east-west, parallel to the Equator; the Equator is 0° latitude and divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres (south of it = Southern Hemisphere); lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole and meet at the poles; the Greenwich (Prime) Meridian is 0° longitude; a latitude-longitude pair gives an exact position.
facts.map-scale: Lesson facts to rely on: scale compares a distance on the map with the real distance on the ground; maps are smaller than the real place so places fit on paper; a line (bar) scale is divided into equal parts (e.g. if one section is 1 km, three sections are 3 km); to find real distance: measure the map distance with a ruler, compare with the scale bar, estimate the real distance in km; large-scale map = small area, more detail (school or town map); small-scale map = large area, less detail (map of Africa, world); one scale applies to the whole map. Ratio scales (e.g. 1:50 000) are not taught here, so avoid them.
facts.locating-places: Lesson facts to rely on: a map grid divides a map into rows and columns; a grid reference says which square holds a place; in a simple letter-number grid the letter is the column and the number is the row (B3 = column B, row 3; C2 = where column C meets row 2); always check the map's own labels; map symbols are small pictures or signs standing for real things (e.g. cross or H for a hospital); the key explains the symbols; symbol shows what a feature is, grid reference shows where.
facts.what-is-trade: Lesson facts to rely on: trade is people, businesses or countries buying and selling goods and services; a service is work done for someone (transport, banking, tourism); an import is brought into a country from another country; an export is sent out of a country to be sold elsewhere (imports come in, exports go out); countries trade because they have different resources, skills, climates, factories and needs, and no country has everything; South African examples: importing oil, exporting fruit or wine; fair, well-managed trade can give income and needed goods.
facts.resources-value: Lesson facts to rely on: resources are things people use from the environment or make with skills and tools; natural resources include minerals, forests, soil, water, sunlight and wind; a resource has value when people need or can use it; value rises when it is scarce (not enough for everyone), useful, good quality or in demand; gold is a mineral that is mined; farmland is valuable because it produces crops and food; processing a resource into a product (e.g. grapes into juice) adds value; resources can be sold or made into goods for trade; sustainable use means using resources carefully so they last for future generations.
facts.fair-trade: Lesson facts to rely on: fair trade means producers (such as farmers and craft workers) get a fair price and safe working conditions when their goods are sold; a producer grows or makes goods, a trader moves or sells them, a customer buys them; fair trade asks if each person in the trade chain is treated fairly; a fair price helps producers cover costs and earn an income; safe conditions protect workers from harm; consumers can support fair trade by asking where products come from, avoiding waste and choosing responsible sellers who respect workers and the environment; local markets let small farmers sell produce.
facts.trade-case-studies: Lesson facts to rely on: South Africa sells exports and buys imports, linking it to Africa and the wider world; international trade is trade between different countries; exports named: minerals (gold), fruit, wine (processed grapes), vehicles/cars (manufactured), some manufactured products; exports can earn income and create jobs; imports named: some oil/fuel, electronics (phones, computers), machinery, medicines; South Africa imports what it does not produce enough of; a trade route is a path used to move goods; goods travel by ship (containers), truck, train and aeroplane via ports and roads; partners shown: EU, China, USA, India.
facts.climate-regions: Lesson facts to rely on: a climate region is an area with similar temperature and rainfall over a long time (climate = long-term pattern; weather changes day to day); climate is described by average temperature and rainfall; climate belts often follow latitude: hot near the Equator, colder towards the poles, because the Sun's rays are less direct near the poles; belts named: tropical, desert, temperate (between hot tropical and cold polar), polar; deserts get very little rainfall; climate affects clothing, homes, farming, water use and transport; Johannesburg gets most rain in summer, Cape Town in winter.
facts.tropical-desert: Lesson facts to rely on: tropical rainforests are found near the Equator and are hot and wet (heavy rainfall) all year; warmth and rain support dense forest with tall trees, vines, insects, birds and animals; the canopy is the leafy upper layer formed by tree crowns, shading lower plants; rainforest plants often have broad leaves to catch light; hot deserts have very little rainfall, extremely hot days and possibly cool nights; desert plants are sparse and save water (spines, thick stems, deep roots, e.g. cacti); desert animals can be active at night to avoid heat; Cairo = hot desert, Manaus (Amazon) = hot and wet all year.
facts.temperate-polar: Lesson facts to rely on: temperate regions are not as hot as the tropics or as cold as polar areas; they often have seasons (warm summers, cool winters) with forests, grasslands, farms and towns; deciduous forests and grasslands occur in some temperate regions; a Mediterranean climate has hot dry summers and mild wet winters, and South Africa's Western Cape is an example; mild means not very cold; Mediterranean plants may have small waxy leaves to reduce water loss; polar climates are near the North and South Poles, very cold with ice or snow most of the year, short growing season, few plants; Moscow is a cool temperate example.
facts.vegetation-adaptations: Lesson facts to rely on: an adaptation is a feature or behaviour that helps a plant or animal survive in its environment; climate affects which adaptations are useful (climate, vegetation, adaptations); desert plants store water in thick stems (cactus) and have spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss and protect them, or deep roots to reach water; rainforest plants have broad leaves to catch light and drip tips for heavy rain; camel stores fat and conserves water; polar animals have thick fur or blubber to keep warm; nocturnal means active at night, so some desert animals avoid daytime heat; Cairo is dry desert, Durban warm and humid.
facts.population-distribution: Lesson facts to rely on: population distribution is how people are spread over an area; dense (densely populated) = many people close together in a small area; sparse (sparsely populated) = few people spread far apart; population density is how many people live in each square kilometre; people settle where there is water, fertile land, jobs, transport, schools and clinics; cities attract people with jobs and services; a new mine or factory can attract people for work; dry deserts, very steep mountains, poor soils and places far from roads or services have fewer people; dots on a map can show distribution.
facts.settlement-patterns: Lesson facts to rely on: a settlement is a place where people live; urban settlements are towns and cities with many buildings, roads, services (shops, factories, offices, schools, hospitals) and high population density; rural settlements are villages, farms and small communities with open land, fewer houses and lower population density; many rural people work in farming, forestry, fishing or tourism, or travel to towns for services not available nearby; urbanisation is the percentage of people living in towns and cities; South Africa has become more urban over time.
facts.migration-push-pull: Lesson facts to rely on: migration means people move from one place to another to live, for a time or permanently; internal migration is within a country (e.g. Limpopo to Gauteng), or people may move between countries; push factors are problems that push people away (drought, floods, conflict, few jobs, poor services, not enough farming land); pull factors attract people to a new place (jobs, schools, clinics, safety, family, better housing, transport); no jobs nearby = push; a factory offering work = pull; better schools elsewhere = pull; jobs are the biggest pull for migrants.
facts.migration-impact: Lesson facts to rely on: migration affects the people who move and the places they leave and enter; positive: migrants bring skills, ideas, languages and cultures, fill jobs, start businesses, send money or support to family at home, help communities grow; challenges: fast city growth needs more housing, water, electricity, transport, schools and clinics; families may miss relatives and need time to adapt to new routines, school, language; places people leave may have fewer working-age adults; net migration positive = province gaining people, negative = losing people; communities should plan housing, jobs and services.
facts.gr6-atlases-global-statistics-t1: Lesson facts to rely on: an atlas is a book of maps; physical maps show mountains, rivers, deserts and oceans; political maps show countries, borders, provinces and cities; theme maps show one topic such as climate or population; the contents page lists the sections with page numbers; the index lists places alphabetically with a page and block reference; the three highest mountains are Mount Everest (about 8 849 m), K2 (about 8 611 m) and Kangchenjunga (about 8 586 m); the Pacific is the biggest ocean, then the Atlantic, then the Indian; all oceans join to make one world ocean; Russia is the largest country by area, then Canada.
facts.gr6-coniferous-forests-t3: Lesson facts to rely on: coniferous forests grow in a belt in the Northern Hemisphere (Canada, Scandinavia, Russia), roughly 50 to 65 degrees north; long very cold winters, short mild summers, rain or snow all year; conifers such as pine, spruce and fir are evergreen with needle leaves and cones, and a sloping shape that sheds snow; animals include wolves, brown bears, moose, lynx and owls; people make a living by logging (timber and paper), hunting and herding reindeer, mining and tourism such as skiing; cut trees should be replaced.
